questions.question: JavaScript in the browser (and Node) is which kind of language?
options: A compiled language: you run a preprocessor, then a linker, like C++.
A scripting language: the engine reads the source and runs it. There is no #include and no separate compile step.
A Python dialect that uses indentation instead of braces.
A typed assembly language for WebAssembly.
questions.explanation: The JS engine interprets (or JIT-compiles internally) the .js file. You do not ship object files. TypeScript is an optional compile-to-JS step.

questions.question: How do you pull in another file of JavaScript? There is no C preprocessor.
options: #include "util.js" at the top of the file.
using Util;
import { foo } from "./util.js"; (or require in older Node).
from util import foo, the same as Python.
questions.explanation: No #include, no #define, no using. Built-ins are global. Your files load with import or require.

questions.question: Which snippet is legal JavaScript?
options: Python-style: for i in range(3) then an indented print(i)
C-like braces: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { console.log(i); }
int i = 0; with a required type on every name.
A .js file must start with #pragma once.
questions.explanation: JS uses braces like C/Java/C#. Indentation is not syntax. Types are not declared on ordinary variables.

questions.question: How do you declare a name you will reassign, and a name you will not?
options: var for both; const is only for classes.
let for a name you reassign; const for a name you will not retarget. Skip var.
int and const int, like C++.
def and final, like Python.
questions.explanation: Default to const. Use let when the name must be retargeted. var is function-scoped and the wrong default.

reference.book: Eloquent JavaScript, 4th Edition by Marijn Haverbeke

questions.question: A binding created with const cannot be retargeted. What else is true of that binding?
options: It is block-scoped, and a grasped object may still mutate.
The value it grasps is frozen; object fields cannot change.
It is function-scoped like var and may be redeclared.
It is hoisted as undefined and can be used before the line.
questions.explanation: const prevents assignment to the name. Objects remain mutable unless you freeze them. const is block-scoped, not function-scoped.

questions.question: What does console.log(Boolean(0), Boolean("0")) print?
options: true true, because both look like zero-ish values that convert to true.
false true, because 0 is falsy and a non-empty string is truthy.
true false, because 0 is an object and "0" is empty.
false false, because both represent the number zero.
questions.explanation: The only falsy number among ordinary numbers is 0. Any non-empty string is truthy, including "0".

questions.question: What is the result of "5" + 1 compared with "5" - 1?
options: Both are 6, because both operators convert to number first.
6 and "51", because - concatenates and + subtracts.
"51" and 4, because + concatenates while - forces numbers.
NaN and NaN, because mixed types always produce NaN.
questions.explanation: + is addition or concatenation and prefers strings. - has no concatenation meaning, so "5" becomes 5.

questions.question: typeof null is "object". How should you test for null?
options: Use typeof value === "object" and treat arrays as null too.
Use value == 0, which is true for null after coercion.
Use !value, which is unique to null and not to 0 or "".
Use value === null, which does not also match undefined.
questions.explanation: typeof null is a historical bug. Strict equality to null is the precise check. !value also catches 0, "", and false.

reference.book: Eloquent JavaScript, 4th Edition by Marijn Haverbeke
reference.excerpt: There are two special values, written null and undefined, that are used to denote the absence of a meaningful value.

questions.question: Number("") and Number(null) and Number(undefined) are:
options: 0, 0, and NaN — empty string and null become 0; undefined does not.
NaN, NaN, and NaN — nothing without digits becomes a number.
0, NaN, and 0 — only null fails while empty string is zero.
undefined, null, and NaN — Number leaves empty values unchanged.
questions.explanation: Number("") is 0, which is why payment parsers must reject empty strings before converting. Number(undefined) is NaN.

array

plain object

questions.question: Why is var a bad default compared with let?
options: var cannot be reassigned, so loops cannot update an index.
var is block-scoped and cannot be seen inside if bodies.
var is function-scoped and leaks out of blocks such as for and if.
var is the only way to bind a number; let is only for objects.
questions.explanation: var ignores block braces and attaches to the enclosing function. let and const stop at the nearest { }.

questions.question: A C++ const int x cannot have its bits changed. What is the closest JS mistake?
options: Avoiding Number() because C++ const forbids conversion.
Using let for numbers because const cannot hold numbers.
Using === because C++ const requires bitwise identity.
Expecting const customer to freeze customer.id as well.
questions.explanation: JS const protects the binding, not the object’s fields. Freeze separately if you need immutability.

questions.question: What does Number.isNaN(Number("due")) tell you when cleaning payment rows?
options: The amount cannot be used as a finite number and should be skipped.
The string was empty, because only "" becomes NaN.
The amount is zero, because invalid money becomes 0.
Number threw, so you must wrap the call in try/catch.
questions.explanation: Number("due") is NaN. Number never throws on ordinary strings. Skip or flag the row; do not add NaN into a total.

questions.question: Which check treats a missing amount and a zero amount as the same?
options: amount === 0, which is true only for numeric zero.
if (amount), which skips 0 as well as null, "", and undefined.
amount == null, which matches null and undefined only.
Number.isFinite(amount), which is true for 0.
questions.explanation: 0 is falsy. A zero-dollar payment is a real business value. Test nullish and finite-number separately.

options: Boolean(raw), because money is true or false.
String(raw), then add it, because totals are text.
raw + 0, because + always yields a number.

questions.question: false == 0 is true. false === 0 is false. What rule should you take from that?
options: Use === unless you have a specific reason to coerce.
Use == for numbers and === for strings only.
Use == always so null and 0 match the same way.
Avoid both and compare with Boolean() on each side.
questions.explanation: == coerces and makes 0, false, and "" look interchangeable. === compares type and value.

questions.question: Which statement about JavaScript numbers is accurate for someone used to C++ int and double?
options: Integer literals are 32-bit ints until they overflow into double.
Everyday arithmetic uses one IEEE-754 number type, not a separate int.
Bigint is the default type for loop indices and array lengths.
Division of two integers always truncates toward zero.
questions.explanation: 1/2 is 0.5. Array length is a number, not bigint. There is no C++-style int default.

questions.question: Strings in JavaScript cannot have a character overwritten in place. What follows?
options: You must use a StringBuilder class from the standard library.
task[0] = "X" mutates a string the same way as a C++ std::string.
Methods such as replace return a new string; the original is unchanged.
const s = "paid" prevents reading s[0] because the string is frozen.
questions.explanation: Primitives are immutable. String methods return new values. Index assignment on a string does not change it in ordinary code.

questions.explanation: A narrow allow-list avoids treating arbitrary strings as true. JSON.parse("yes") throws.
